issue.title: Variance of generics
issue.body:
It should be possible to define a type variable as covariant. For example, the type variable of Iterable[t] could be covariant, and then Iterable[x] would a subtype of Iterable[y] if x is a subtype of y. Currently this is not the case, which is sometimes awkward, and this would even more awkward with union types.

Not sure about the syntax. Maybe something like this:

```
T = typevar('T', covariant=True)   
```

(Ouch, looks pretty technical.)

Covariant type variables must not appear within method argument types or instance variable types, i.e. they are only valid as return types. Also, only read-only properties can have types with covariant type variables.

issue.title: Reject covariant overriding of attributes
issue.body:
Covariant overriding of attributes is allowed though it's clearly unsafe. Example:
```py
class A:
    x: float

class B(A):
    x: int  # no error, though unsafe

def f(a: A) -> None:
    a.x = 1.1

b = B()
f(b)
b.x  # float at runtime, though declared as int
```

Mypy should reject `x: int` in `B`. If this is actually what the programmer intended, they can use `# type: ignore`.

body:
Am I correct in thinking that an example of this issue is:
```py
from typing import TypeVar, Generic
T = TypeVar("T", covariant=True)
class Foo(Generic[T]):
    foo: T
a: Foo[int] = Foo()
b: Foo[object] = a
b.foo = "sus"
a.foo + 1  # no mypy error, runtime error
```

issue.title: Reject more covariant overrides
issue.body:
Follow up to #3208. We should also reject things like:
```
from typing import TypeVar, Generic
T = TypeVar("T", covariant=True)
class Foo(Generic[T]):
    def __init__(self, value: T) -> None:
        self.foo = value
```

issue.title: Check variance on pre-3.12 `TypeVar`s

repository.name: basedpyright
repository.description: pyright fork with various type checking improvements, improved vscode support and pylance features built into the language server

issue.body:
### Description

See:
https://github.com/DetachHead/basedpyright/issues/763
https://github.com/DetachHead/basedpyright/issues/395
https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/735
https://discuss.python.org/t/why-do-type-checkers-not-warn-when-incorrect-variance-is-used/104668

Type checkers don't warn when incorrect variance is used with old-style `TypeVar`s.

```py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import TypeVar, Generic

T_co = TypeVar("T_co", covariant=True)

@dataclass
class OldDataclass(Generic[T_co]):
    x: T_co  # error expected, not reported
    y: list[T_co]  # error expected, not reported

class OldBox(Generic[T_co]):
    def __init__(self, value: T_co) -> None:
        self.value: T_co = value  # error expected, not reported

class OldShelf(Generic[T_co]):
    def __init__(self, values: list[T_co]) -> None:
        self._values: list[T_co] = values

    def get_values(self) -> list[T_co]:  # error expected, not reported
        return self._values

    def set_values(self, new_values: list[T_co]) -> None:  # error expected, not reported
        self._values = new_values
```

From the discourse thread, pyright copied this bug from mypy. I think it's going to cause pain for people when they migrate from `TypeVar` to the modern syntax and only then realize that they used the wrong variance for their generic class all along. And, of course, it's just unsound.
I propose two alternate solutions:

1. Add an optional diagnostic rule for `covariant=` and `contravariant=` parameters on `TypeVar`. If you need to support Python 3.10 and 3.11 (or 3.12 and you want `default`), use `typing_extensions.TypeVar` with `infer_variance=True` instead. This should be pretty easy to implement.
2. Actually validate the variance. Just pretend `infer_variance` is on instead of `covariant=` or `contravariant=`, and show an error if the inferred variance doesn't match the stated variance. Not sure how difficult it would be to implement. The error will be confusing because it doesn't say why the variance is wrong. But I guess that's not any worse than new-style type variables that don't tell you why they're invariant.
